tweets.text: We’ll start the week with some brand-new portfolio updates, but I’m going to take it easy this weekend. I’ve spent a lot of time following the markets all week, so now that the markets are closed, it’s time to relax and clear my head a little.

July jobs report is out, and it came in well below expectations. • Nonfarm payrolls: -23K (expected +85K) • Unemployment: 4.1% (expected 4.2%) • Average hourly earnings: +3.2% YoY The real issue is the revisions. May: 129K → 63K, June: 57K → 20K. That’s a combined downward revision of 103K over the two months. Unemployment looks better, but for the wrong reason. The labor force participation rate fell to 61.4%, down 0.7 percentage points since January. In other words, the rate is falling not because people are finding jobs, but because they’re leaving the labor force. Those on temporary layoff also rose by 153K to 921K. Sectors: local government education -50K, retail -19K, financial activities -14K. Healthcare was the only sector holding up, adding 22K jobs. The picture has changed ahead of the Fed’s September meeting.

If you’re between 18 and 25, don’t build your life around nothing but partying and consumption. Take a step back from parties, showing off, and instant gratification. Save your money. Learn how to invest. Don’t underestimate small amounts of money. Think in terms of 7–8 years. Learn how even the amounts that seem insignificant today can grow into something meaningful over time when you consistently save and invest wisely. During this journey, people may tell you: “You’re being too hard on yourself.” “You’re young. Enjoy your life.” “You’re too selfish when it comes to money.” “Why are you worrying about this at your age?” You don’t have to listen to them. Because most people will teach you to live only for today. They will normalize consuming more, spending more, and putting everything you earn back into the system. You can choose a different path. You can consume a little less today, save a little more, and learn how to invest and build financial freedom. The goal isn’t to look rich. The goal is to actually become wealthy. The goal isn’t to prove anything to anyone. It’s to make sure that, in the future, you have control over your own life. If you’re 18–25, you don’t have to spend every dollar you earn. Your biggest advantage at this age isn’t your money. It’s your time. Use it. Start small. Stay consistent. Be patient. Learn the power of compound growth. The small steps you take today could become one of the biggest differences in your life 7–8 years from now. And perhaps most importantly: Wealth isn’t built overnight. It’s built through habits that can create financial security not just for you, but for generations to come.

$AAOI 2Q26 — what happens if the targets are hit? Q2 revenue was $191.9M, up 86% YoY. 800G revenue hit $12.8M, more than 10x YoY and more than 2x QoQ. 400G was $48.4M. But the headline $0.06 non-GAAP EPS is misleading: non-GAAP operating loss was $10.3M and adjusted EBITDA was -$0.5M. A $13M tax benefit pushed net income positive. The “return to profitability” was largely accounting-driven. The real story is capacity. Management says monthly production capacity is approaching 200K units today, rising to 650K+ by year-end 2026 and 930K+ by year-end 2027. The key target: by mid-2027, monthly datacenter transceiver revenue of ~$471M: • 100G/400G: ~$90M • 800G: ~$217M • 1.6T: ~$164M That implies ~$5.65B annualized datacenter revenue. Add CATV and other products, and the run-rate could reach ~$6.1B. The math is internally consistent: ~$471M/month implies roughly 780K transceivers/month, broadly in line with the planned capacity ramp. But there’s a catch. To hit the company’s ~$1.1B 2026 revenue target, Q4 revenue needs to be roughly $484M — a 78% sequential jump from Q3 guidance. The breakdown works: ~$330M from 800G + 1.6T, ~$115M CATV and ~$40M legacy products. But there is essentially no room for execution errors. And profitability is the bigger question. Using management’s guidance, I estimate 2026 non-GAAP operating profit at roughly $59M — less than half of the $140M+ target management cited in May. That $140M figure was not repeated on the Q2 call. Near-term gross margin guidance has also moved toward 32–33%, versus the previous 35% year-end target and 40%+ target for 2027. If the ~$6.1B revenue run-rate is achieved, the economics become very interesting. At 30–40% gross margins, my rough model produces ~$1.1–1.65B of net income, or roughly $10–15 EPS on 110M shares. At $124.22, that implies roughly 8–12x forward P/E. A 12.5 EPS scenario would imply: 15x → ~$190 20x → ~$250 25x → ~$310 30x → ~$375 But there are three major risks. Dilution. Weighted shares are already up 43.7% YoY. AAOI has raised $538.8M through the ATM, while Q2 capex was $565.5M. If shares reach 125M, EPS falls ~12% versus the 110M-share model. Supply constraints. DSP and TIA availability are limiting 1.6T shipments. Q4 1.6T revenue may be capped at $70–80M despite higher demand. Customer concentration. The top 10 customers account for 99% of revenue, while one CATV customer represents 42%. So my takeaway: This is not a demand story anymore. It’s an execution story. The market already knows the demand is there. The question is whether AAOI can ramp capacity from ~200K to 930K units/month, secure the components, maintain 33%+ margins and do it without massive dilution. The quarter to watch is Q4’26. ~$485M revenue → thesis gets validated. $380–400M → the entire 2027 model likely gets pushed out. That’s the setup.

BofA initiated coverage of $TSEM with a Buy rating and a $367 price target. Analyst Oliver Wong’s thesis, in short: Tower is the market leader in SiPho PIC manufacturing for pluggable transceivers used in AI data centers. He expects SiPho revenue to double in 2026, with growth continuing through 2027 and beyond. He forecasts 62% CAGR in EBITDA from 2025–28, with his 2027 and 2028 EPS estimates 13% and 28% above consensus, respectively. Looking at the company’s actual numbers, the thesis isn’t without substance. Q2 revenue came in at $460 million, up 24% YoY. Gross profit was $138 million, operating profit $90 million, and net income $90.8 million, or $0.80 per share — versus $0.42 in the same quarter last year. Q3 guidance is $520 million (±5%), implying 31% YoY growth. The key number: SiPho’s annualized revenue run-rate has increased from $180 million to $680 million. That’s nearly 4x in one year. There’s also visibility. Tower has a signed $1.3 billion SiPho contract for 2027, along with $290 million in capacity reservation prepayments. If the customer has put the money down upfront, that’s not just a demand forecast — it’s a commitment. In Japan, Tower announced a $3 billion capacity investment backed by approximately $1 billion in support from METI. The company has raised its 2028 model to $3.6 billion in revenue and $1.2 billion in net income. My takeaway: the thesis here is not demand, but capacity and timing. The Arai facility is expected to be ready for full production in Q4 2027. Everything that can be produced is already being sold up to that point. That’s also where the risk lies: if there’s a delay, the 2028 model gets pushed back as well. Then there’s the valuation. The stock has reached a $27 billion market cap. Most of the good news is already priced in. At $367, the stock is essentially pricing in Tower hitting its 2028 targets on time. One caveat: I couldn’t independently verify BofA’s report or the $367 price target — it didn’t show up in my searches. The company’s reported figures and the Japan investment are verified, but I’d confirm the BofA report through a source such as Fly or TipRanks before publishing.

$AAOI Q2 2026 — Record Revenue Looks Great, But Margins and Dilution Are the Real Story AAOI posted $191.9 million in revenue for the second quarter. Same quarter last year was $103 million, last quarter was $151.1 million. Datacenter climbed to $107.7 million from $44.8 million a year ago, and CATV came in at $80.6 million. Fifth record quarter in a row. The headline number looks good. I went underneath it. Margins went backwards. GAAP gross margin was 27.7%. It was 30.3% a year ago and 29.1% last quarter. Non-GAAP was 29.8%. Revenue nearly doubled and margin still slipped. That’s fixed cost absorption during a capacity build and production yields that haven’t settled yet. Normal for a ramp, but it isn’t the picture the “AI demand is exploding” narrative sets you up to expect. The quality of the profit. The headline shows $5.5 million in non-GAAP net income and $0.06 EPS. Sitting inside that number is a $14.3 million tax-related adjustment. In the same quarter, adjusted EBITDA was negative $0.5 million and the GAAP net loss was $22.8 million, or $0.28 per share. The company hasn’t started generating cash yet. It reached the profit line through accounting. Those are two different things. The part nobody’s talking about: dilution. Basic share count is now 81.6 million, up from 56.8 million a year ago. Paid-in capital went from $1.22 billion to $2.19 billion. Cash rose from $216 million to $508.8 million, and the source of that wasn’t operations, it was equity issuance. Revenue grew 86% while revenue per share grew roughly 31%. Existing shareholders financed part of that growth. On the balance sheet, PP&E went from $376 million to $697 million, inventories from $183 million to $278.8 million, receivables from $244 million to $314 million. The investment is real. If it converts, excellent. If it doesn’t, it was expensive. What management said Q3 guidance is $255-290 million in revenue, 29-30.5% non-GAAP margin, EPS of $0.11-0.26 on 92.8 million shares. The midpoint is $272 million, roughly 42% sequential growth. Capacity is approaching 200,000 units a month, targeting 650,000 by year-end and 930,000 by the end of 2027. On 100G there’s a $20-25 million hit from a memory-related switch shortage, which they expect to clear in a few months. The $200 million-plus 1.6T order starts shipping very late in Q3 and lands mostly in Q4, with 800G and 1.6T combined running around $330 million in Q4. Thompson Lin is guiding to 32-33% margin near term, with more upside as 1.6T mix builds. Here’s where I put my note The full-year target of $1.1 billion is unchanged. First half came in at $343 million. Q3 midpoint is $272 million. That leaves about $485 million for Q4, which is 78% sequential growth. Even stacking CATV and legacy products on top of management’s own $330 million 800G/1.6T figure, you only get to $1.1 billion if everything goes perfectly. No line delays, no hiccups in laser or indium phosphide supply. There’s also an option here: the debate over a ban on Chinese transceivers. Management calls it early but acknowledges U.S. manufacturing is already what pulls customers in. In that scenario the strategic value of the Texas build rises sharply. My take: demand isn’t the problem, production and supply are the entire problem. The story is real, but the multiple has already priced the story. For a company still running EBITDA below zero, the margin for error is thin. I’ll be watching shipments rather than narrative: does Q4 delivery hold, and does margin actually get to 32%.
